newsitem.title: USA: Excel to buy Telco for $1.2 billion.
newsitem.headline: Excel to buy Telco for $1.2 billion.

text.p: Excel Communications Inc. said Friday it agreed to buy Telco Communications Group Inc. for $1.2 billion to strengthen its position as the fifth largest long-distance company in the United States.

The deal will create a communications company with 6.3 million customers, a 100,000-mile fiber optic network and revenues of about $2 billion, and generate substantial cost savings for Excel, officials said.
Excel stock jumped $2.125 to $20.875 in late trading on the New York Stock Exchange, and Telco stock jumped $3.875 to $25.875 on the Nasdaq market.

"This merger represents a significant strategic move for Excel as we continue to implement our vision of becoming a leading provider of communications products both domestically and internationally," Excel Chairman Kenny Troutt said in a statement.
Industry analysts said the acquisition will provide Dallas-based Excel with the network it needed to continue growing and should also boost profit margins.
Formed just 10 years ago, Excel had carved a niche by buying wholesale long-distance service from companies with networks and reselling it to customers through independent sales agents.
That strategy brought sensational growth rates, with revenues rising from $31.2 million in 1993 to $1.32 billion in 1996, but the company decided it was time to set up its own long-distance network.
"Once you have a critical mass of traffic, you are better off having your own network," said Harry Blount, an analyst at Rauscher Pierce Refsnes. "They had reached that point."
He said the deal should boost Excel's profit margins by five to 10 percentage points and raised his 1998 earnings per share estimate to $1.80 from $1.53.
Jack McLaine, Excel's executive vice president, said he expected 1998 earnings to rise to $1.80 to $2.20 a share.
Excel had 1996 net income of $1.35 per share or $144.4 million.

McLaine told Reuters Excel would realise cost savings in excess of $100 million in 1998. "It is basically going to reduce our transmission costs, our communication costs, by about 20 percent, between 1.5 cents and 2.0 cents per minute."
"That's another benefit of this: there is no guesswork," McLaine said, adding that it would take two years to shift all of Excel's traffic onto the Telco network.

Troutt said the acquisition would also better position the combined company as it looks to enter the $100 billion local telephone market and ultimately provide a bundled package of local, long-distance and wireless services.
Telco currently offers discounted long-distance telephone services, mainly through two plans, Dial and Save and Long Distance Wholesale Club.
Under the agreement, Telco shareholders will receive 0.7595 share of common stock of the combined company and $15 in cash for each share of Telco common stock.
Excel shareholders will receive one share of the new company for each share of Excel common stock. Upon completion of the merger, Excel shareholders will own about 80 percent of the new company.
The transaction will be accounted for as a purchase, with the stock portion expected to be tax-free to shareholders of both companies, Excel said.
The merger agreement, approved by directors of both companies, is expected to close by the end of the year.
The current Telco management team will remain in place and Telco will keep its headquarters in Chantilly, Va.
